lessonTitle: Gastroenterology and Renal Disease in Children: Abdominal and Urinary Problems

blocks.text: A 5-week-old boy vomits his whole feed so forcefully that it lands a metre away. The vomit is milky, never green, and a minute later he is ravenous and rooting again. His weight has fallen below his birth centile. What is the anatomical problem, what happens to his blood chemistry, and why must he be rehydrated before any operation?

blocks.markdown: Vomiting and abdominal pain in infants have a wide differential, from trivial (gastro-oesophageal reflux, overfeeding) to surgical emergencies. Urinary and renal problems are also common and often silent. In this unit we separate surgical from medical causes of infant vomiting and abdominal pain, describe how urinary tract infection (UTI) is diagnosed and managed, and recognise nephrotic syndrome and post-infectious glomerulonephritis.

blocks.title: Colour of the vomit and the pattern of pain guide urgency
blocks.text: Bilious (green) vomiting in an infant is a surgical emergency until proven otherwise. Non-bilious projectile vomiting with hunger suggests pyloric stenosis. Intermittent severe colicky pain with pallor suggests intussusception. A well infant with effortless 'happy spitting' and normal growth usually has benign reflux.

blocks.markdown: **Pyloric stenosis** is hypertrophy of the pyloric circular muscle that obstructs gastric outflow, presenting in the first weeks of life, more commonly in first-born boys. Vomiting is non-bilious because the obstruction lies proximal to the duodenal ampulla. Repeated loss of gastric hydrochloric acid produces a **hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis**; volume depletion from vomiting drives the kidney to retain sodium (via aldosterone), and it does so by excreting potassium and hydrogen ions, so the urine becomes paradoxically acidic despite the systemic alkalosis. Signs include visible gastric peristalsis and a palpable 'olive' in the right upper abdomen during a test feed. Diagnosis is by abdominal ultrasound. Treatment is **resuscitation first** with intravenous fluids and correction of electrolytes, then surgical pyloromyotomy; operating on an alkalotic infant risks post-operative apnoea. Check fluid prescriptions against current local guidance.

**Intussusception** occurs when one segment of bowel telescopes into the next, most often at the ileocaecal region, typically in infants and young children. It causes obstruction and ischaemia. Features: sudden severe **colicky pain** with drawing up of the legs, pallor and lethargy between episodes, vomiting (which may become bilious), a sausage-shaped abdominal mass, and later **redcurrant jelly stool** (blood and mucus). Ultrasound shows the characteristic target (doughnut) sign. A haemodynamically stable child without peritonitis is usually treated by image-guided air or contrast enema reduction; surgery is for failed reduction, perforation or peritonitis. Resuscitation and analgesia come first.

rows: Usually improves with time; red flags absent
Hungry after vomiting; weight loss; olive mass; alkalosis

blocks.title: Interpreting urine tests in a toddler with fever
blocks.prompt: A 20-month-old girl has a temperature of 39 C for two days with no cough or rash. She is feeding less. A clean-catch urine dipstick shows leucocyte esterase positive and nitrite positive. What do you do and why?

steps.text: Principle: in young children UTI presents non-specifically (fever, vomiting, poor feeding, irritability); no source of fever should prompt a urine test.

Interpret dipstick: leucocyte esterase indicates pyuria and nitrite indicates conversion of nitrate by gram-negative bacteria such as Escherichia coli; both positive makes UTI likely, but NICE advises sending a culture before treatment where possible.
Treat according to local antibiotic guidance (check NICE and BNFc), choosing the route by how unwell the child is, and review the culture and sensitivities.

Plan follow-up and imaging: ultrasound is considered for infants and children with atypical or recurrent UTI under NICE guidance; look for structural abnormality such as vesicoureteric reflux or hydronephrosis.

blocks.answer: Likely UTI: send culture, start antibiotics per local guidance, and arrange imaging only where NICE criteria (atypical or recurrent infection) are met.

blocks.markdown:
**Renal disease.** The glomerulus filters plasma through a barrier of endothelium, basement membrane and podocytes. Two syndromes arise when it is injured:

- **Nephrotic syndrome**: heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema (with hyperlipidaemia). In children the commonest cause is **minimal change disease**, which responds to corticosteroids. Presentation: periorbital oedema in the morning, then generalised swelling and frothy urine. Complications: infection (especially peritonitis), thrombosis and hypovolaemia.
- **Nephritic syndrome**: inflammation causing haematuria, hypertension, oliguria and mild oedema. **Post-infectious (post-streptococcal) glomerulonephritis** occurs after a latent period following throat or skin infection with certain group A streptococcal strains. It presents with cola-coloured urine, oedema and hypertension, with low serum complement C3, and is usually self-limiting with supportive care. Check treatment details against current guidance.

blocks.caption: Urine protein:creatinine ratio, a spot-urine measure of proteinuria. Interpretation cut-offs differ between guidelines and laboratories.

blocks.title: Calculating a protein:creatinine ratio
blocks.prompt: A 4-year-old with puffy eyes has a spot urine with protein 900 mg/L and creatinine 3.0 mmol/L. Calculate the PCR and say what the pattern of findings would support.

steps.text: Interpretation: a ratio of this magnitude is heavy proteinuria, in the nephrotic range by commonly used thresholds (check your local laboratory's reference).
With periorbital oedema, low serum albumin and no haematuria or hypertension, this supports minimal change nephrotic syndrome, usually treated with corticosteroids after specialist guidance.
Counsel on infection risk and arrange monitoring for relapses.

blocks.answer: PCR 300 mg/mmol, consistent with nephrotic-range proteinuria.

blocks.caption: Nephrotic versus nephritic presentations
rows: Heavy proteinuria, frothy, no visible blood
Supportive: fluid, salt restriction, blood pressure control

items: Weigh and plot growth in any vomiting infant; assess hydration.
Always record the colour of vomit and stool.
Send a urine sample in any febrile young child with no clear source.
Check blood pressure in any child with haematuria or oedema.
Know when to call surgeons: bilious vomit, peritonism, bloody stool, shock.

blocks.title: Do not give up on a hungry vomiting baby
blocks.text: In pyloric stenosis the infant looks well between feeds, and parents may be told it is reflux. Persistent projectile vomiting with faltering weight deserves senior review and electrolytes.

points: Distinguish infant vomiting by vomit colour and pattern: pyloric stenosis (projectile, non-bilious, alkalosis, fluid correction before surgery) versus intussusception (colicky pain, pallor, redcurrant jelly stool, ultrasound and enema).
Diagnose UTI from a properly collected urine sample with culture, treat by local guidance, and use imaging selectively according to NICE criteria.
Nephrotic syndrome (proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema) is usually steroid-responsive minimal change disease; post-infectious glomerulonephritis presents with haematuria, hypertension and low C3.

questions.stem: A 6-week-old boy has projectile non-bilious vomiting after every feed and a weak weight gain. A venous blood gas would most likely show which pattern?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: loss of gastric acid causes alkalosis with low chloride and potassium.
distractorRationale.b: Hyperchloraemic acidosis follows diarrhoea or renal bicarbonate loss.
distractorRationale.c: Respiratory alkalosis is not expected and hyperkalaemia does not occur.

questions.explanation: Repeated loss of hydrochloric acid in vomit raises plasma bicarbonate and lowers chloride, while volume depletion drives aldosterone-mediated sodium retention in the kidney, which excretes potassium and hydrogen ions, so the urine is paradoxically acidic despite systemic alkalosis. Correction of this derangement is needed before pyloromyotomy.

questions.stem: A 10-month-old has had three episodes of sudden screaming with drawing up of the legs, lasting minutes, each followed by pallor and drowsiness. A stool contains blood and mucus. What is the most likely diagnosis?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: colicky pain with pallor between attacks and bloody mucus stool.
distractorRationale.b: Pyloric stenosis presents earlier with projectile vomiting.
distractorRationale.c: Reflux is not associated with blood and mucus stool or episodic severe pain.

questions.explanation: The intermittent colic and redcurrant jelly stool reflect bowel telescoping with venous congestion and mucosal bleeding. Ultrasound confirms it and stable children are treated by enema reduction.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl has fever and dysuria. A properly collected urine sample is positive for leucocyte esterase and nitrite. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Send urine for culture and start antibiotics according to local guidance, reviewing sensitivities
Wait for culture before any treatment regardless of severity
Treat with antibiotics and never culture

questions.correctOptionText: Send urine for culture and start antibiotics according to local guidance, reviewing sensitivities

distractorRationale.a: Correct: culture guides therapy and treatment is not delayed in a symptomatic child.
distractorRationale.b: Delay is inappropriate when UTI is likely and the child is symptomatic.
distractorRationale.c: Culture is needed to confirm and tailor treatment.
distractorRationale.d: Routine prophylaxis is not recommended for a first UTI.

questions.explanation: A positive nitrite and leucocyte esterase makes UTI likely, so culture is sent and treatment started without waiting for results. The antibiotic and route follow current NICE and local guidance.

questions.stem: Which child with a urinary tract infection should most clearly be considered for renal tract ultrasound according to common guidance such as NICE (verify the local protocol)?

options.text: Every child after a first uncomplicated lower UTI that responds promptly
A child with a negative urine culture and a viral illness
A child with a single positive dipstick and no symptoms

distractorRationale.a: Correct: recurrent or atypical UTI warrants imaging for structural abnormality.
distractorRationale.b: Uncomplicated, quickly responsive first UTI in older children usually does not need routine imaging.
distractorRationale.d: Asymptomatic dipstick positivity is not an indication.

questions.explanation: Imaging looks for structural causes such as obstruction or vesicoureteric reflux, so it targets atypical or recurrent infection. Exact criteria depend on age and guideline version and should be checked.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old has had a sore throat treated two weeks ago. He now has dark cola-coloured urine, puffy eyelids and a blood pressure above the expected range for age. Complement C3 is low. What is the most likely diagnosis?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: haematuria, hypertension and low C3 after a streptococcal infection.
distractorRationale.b: Minimal change disease has heavy proteinuria, normal C3 and no haematuria.
distractorRationale.c: UTI does not cause hypertension or low C3.

questions.explanation: Immune complex deposition after streptococcal infection activates complement and inflames glomeruli, giving nephritic features. Management is supportive and most children recover.

questions.stem: True or false: in a child with nephrotic syndrome, the main complications to anticipate include serious infection and thrombosis.
questions.explanation: Loss of immunoglobulins and clotting regulators in urine, plus hypovolaemia and steroids, raises risk of infection and thrombosis. Families should know to seek help for fever or abdominal pain.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old with periorbital oedema has a spot urine with protein 1650 mg/L and creatinine 5.0 mmol/L. Calculate the urine protein:creatinine ratio in mg/mmol.
questions.explanation: The ratio equals protein concentration divided by creatinine concentration, 1650 / 5.0 = 330 mg/mmol. Laboratories quote their own interpretation thresholds, but this value indicates heavy proteinuria.

questions.stem: A 5-week-old infant weighed 3.80 kg at his last clinic visit and now weighs 3.42 kg after a week of persistent vomiting. What is his percentage weight loss relative to the earlier weight?
questions.explanation: Weight lost is 3.80 minus 3.42, or 0.38 kg. Dividing by 3.80 gives 0.10, which is 10%, a substantial loss in an infant that warrants prompt assessment of hydration and electrolytes.

questions.stem: Compare pyloric stenosis with intussusception in infants in terms of typical presentation, investigation and initial management.
markingGuide: Pyloric stenosis: projectile non-bilious vomiting after feeds in first weeks, hungry after vomiting, weight loss, olive mass
Pyloric stenosis: ultrasound, hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis; fluid and electrolyte correction then pyloromyotomy
Intussusception: episodic colicky pain with drawing up of legs, pallor between episodes, redcurrant jelly stool, sausage mass
Intussusception: ultrasound target sign; resuscitation, analgesia and air or contrast enema reduction if stable; surgery if peritonitis or failed reduction
Bilious vomiting in either setting is a red flag for urgent surgical review
questions.explanation: Both cause vomiting, but the pattern, age, stool and metabolic consequences differ. Management differs: pyloric stenosis needs resuscitation then surgery, whereas intussusception is usually first reduced non-operatively.

questions.stem: Explain how you would distinguish nephrotic syndrome from post-infectious glomerulonephritis in a child with swelling, and outline the principal management approach for each.
markingGuide: Nephrotic: heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, marked oedema, normal blood pressure, no visible haematuria
Nephritic: haematuria, hypertension, oliguria, mild oedema, low C3, preceding streptococcal infection
Nephrotic: usually minimal change disease, corticosteroids, vigilance for infection and thrombosis
Post-infectious GN: supportive, fluid and salt control, blood pressure treatment, monitor renal function, usually self-limiting
Urine tests, blood tests (albumin, creatinine, C3) and blood pressure guide the distinction
questions.explanation: The pattern of urine findings and blood pressure shows which part of glomerular function is disturbed. Distinguishing them guides treatment, since steroids are used for minimal change nephrotic syndrome but not for post-infectious glomerulonephritis.
